question: What is the primary pathophysiology underlying the development of peptic ulcer disease?

options.A: An increase in mucosal blood flow throughout the gastrointestinal tract
options.B: An imbalance between aggressive mucosal factors and defensive mucosal mechanisms
options.C: Overproduction of protective bicarbonate by the gastric mucosa
options.D: Permanent hyperplasia of the intestinal villi in the duodenum

explanation: PUD develops when aggressive factors like gastric acid and H. pylori overwhelm the defensive mucosal mechanisms of the stomach and duodenum. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T1#GNS223_U3_T1_h1)

question: Which of the following is a primary goal of pharmacological treatment in peptic ulcer disease?

options.A: To accelerate the rate of gastric emptying permanently
options.B: To relieve abdominal pain and promote ulcer healing
options.C: To stimulate continuous pepsinogen secretion in the stomach

explanation: The main aims of treatment are to alleviate patient discomfort, heal the mucosal sores, and prevent dangerous complications like bleeding and perforation. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T1#GNS223_U3_T1_h1)

question: Which cellular structure acts as the final common pathway for the secretion of hydrogen ions into the gastric lumen?
explanation: The H+/K+ ATPase pump (proton pump) on the parietal cell membrane is the final common pathway responsible for pumping hydrogen ions into the stomach. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T1#GNS223_U3_T1_h2)

question: What is the primary physiological role of prostaglandins in the gastric mucosa?

options.A: To stimulate excessive production of hydrochloric acid
options.B: To inhibit the secretion of protective mucus and bicarbonate
options.C: To maintain mucosal defenses by promoting mucus and bicarbonate production
options.D: To block the microvascular blood supply to the stomach lining

explanation: Prostaglandins protect the gastric lining by stimulating mucus and bicarbonate production and enhancing mucosal blood flow. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T1#GNS223_U3_T1_h2)

question: What is the exact mechanism of action of Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs)?

options.A: Competitive antagonism of histamine H2-receptors on parietal cells
options.B: Irreversible inhibition of the H+/K+ ATPase enzyme pump
options.C: Direct chemical neutralization of hydrochloric acid in the stomach lumen
options.D: Stimulation of prostaglandin E2 synthesis in surface epithelial cells

explanation: PPIs work by irreversibly binding to and inhibiting the H+/K+ ATPase enzyme pump, shutting down the final step of acid secretion. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T1#GNS223_U3_T1_h3)

question: When is the optimal time for a nurse to administer oral Proton Pump Inhibitors to a patient?

options.A: Right before going to bed at night
options.B: Immediately after consuming the largest meal of the day
options.C: 30 to 60 minutes before the first meal of the day
options.D: Concurrently with antacids for immediate relief

explanation: PPIs are most effective when given 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast, as this aligns with the maximal activation of proton pumps following overnight fasting. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T1#GNS223_U3_T1_h3)

question: How do H2-Receptor Antagonists exert their therapeutic effects on gastric acid?

options.A: By irreversibly destroying the H+/K+ ATPase enzyme pump
options.B: By competitively and reversibly blocking histamine H2-receptors on parietal cells
options.C: By physically coating the gastric mucosa with a protective barrier
options.D: By directly neutralizing secreted hydrochloric acid in the stomach lumen

explanation: H2RAs work through competitive and reversible blockade of H2 receptors on parietal cells, preventing histamine from stimulating acid production. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T1#GNS223_U3_T1_h4)

question: Which H2RA is well-known for inhibiting hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes and causing potential drug interactions?
explanation: Cimetidine inhibits the cytochrome P450 system, which can impair the metabolism of other drugs and lead to toxicity. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T1#GNS223_U3_T1_h4)

question: What is the primary mechanism of action of antacids in the gastrointestinal tract?

options.A: Inhibition of the proton pump on parietal cell membranes
options.B: Direct chemical neutralization of hydrochloric acid in the stomach lumen
options.C: Eradication of Helicobacter pylori bacteria via antimicrobial action
options.D: Stimulation of gastric prostaglandin synthesis for mucosal repair

explanation: Antacids are basic compounds that chemically react with and neutralize existing gastric acid to quickly raise stomach pH. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T1#GNS223_U3_T1_h5)

question: Why is it important for nurses to advise patients to separate antacids from other oral medications by 1-2 hours?

options.A: Antacids speed up gastric motility and will wash other drugs away
options.B: Antacids can alter the absorption of other drugs or bind to them
options.C: Concurrent administration causes severe immediate hypertension
options.D: Other drugs will completely neutralize the therapeutic effects of antacids

explanation: Antacids can bind to other drugs or change gastric pH, which interferes with their absorption, necessitating a timed separation. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T1#GNS223_U3_T1_h5)

question: Which combination of antacid ingredients is commonly used to balance adverse gastrointestinal effects?
explanation: Magnesium causes diarrhea and aluminum causes constipation, so combining them helps neutralize each other's effects on bowel motility. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T1#GNS223_U3_T1_h5)

question: How does sucralfate protect an ulcerated gastric or duodenal mucosa?

options.A: By completely neutralizing all hydrochloric acid in the stomach lumen
options.B: By forming a sticky, gel-like barrier that binds directly to exposed ulcer craters
options.C: By killing Helicobacter pylori bacteria through systemic antibiotic action
options.D: By blocking histamine receptors on the basolateral membrane of parietal cells

explanation: In an acidic environment, sucralfate forms a viscous paste that selectively adheres to ulcer craters to protect them from acid and pepsin. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T1#GNS223_U3_T1_h6)

question: Why is misoprostol strictly contraindicated for use in pregnant women?

options.A: It causes severe and irreversible maternal hypertension
options.B: It acts as a potent uterine stimulant that can induce abortion or premature labor
options.C: It permanently deactivates fetal liver enzymes during development
options.D: It completely halts fetal bone formation and calcification

explanation: Misoprostol stimulates uterine contractions, making it dangerous for pregnant patients due to the high risk of miscarriage or premature birth. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T1#GNS223_U3_T1_h6)

question: Why is the eradication of Helicobacter pylori essential in the management of peptic ulcer disease?

options.A: It permanently prevents the stomach from ever producing gastric acid again
options.B: It reduces ulcer recurrence rates to near zero by eliminating the underlying pathogen
options.C: It acts as a potent antacid that immediately neutralizes luminal pH
options.D: It stimulates the rapid regeneration of pancreatic digestive enzymes

explanation: Treating H. pylori removes the root cause of chronic mucosal inflammation, which drastically lowers the chance of ulcers coming back. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T1#GNS223_U3_T1_h7)

question: What does standard bismuth quadruple therapy for H. pylori eradication typically include?

options.A: A PPI, clarithromycin, amoxicillin, and metronidazole
options.B: A PPI, bismuth subsalicylate, tetracycline, and metronidazole
options.C: An H2RA, two antacids, and a mucosal protectant
options.D: Misoprostol, sucralfate, and a single broad-spectrum antibiotic

explanation: Bismuth quadruple therapy combines a PPI, bismuth subsalicylate, tetracycline, and metronidazole to effectively target resistant H. pylori strains. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T1#GNS223_U3_T1_h7)

question: Which lifestyle modification should a nurse strongly emphasize to a patient being treated for peptic ulcer disease?

options.A: Increasing the daily intake of caffeinated beverages to stimulate digestion
options.B: Smoking cessation, as nicotine decreases bicarbonate secretion and delays healing
options.C: Engaging in strenuous physical exercise immediately after eating
options.D: Eliminating all forms of dietary protein to rest the gastrointestinal tract

explanation: Nicotine impairs protective mucosal defenses like bicarbonate secretion and slows down ulcer healing, making cessation vital. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T1#GNS223_U3_T1_h8)

question: What is an important nursing responsibility when caring for a patient prescribed an anti-ulcer drug regimen that includes bismuth subsalicylate?

options.A: Warn the patient that bismuth will permanently turn their urine bright red
options.B: Inform the patient that harmless black discoloration of the stool is expected
options.C: Advise the patient to stop taking the drug immediately if diarrhea occurs
options.D: Instruct the patient to take the bismuth tablet on an empty stomach with an antacid

explanation: Bismuth reacts with sulfur in the digestive tract to form a harmless black compound that darkens the stool, which can alarm patients if not forewarned. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T1#GNS223_U3_T1_h8)
